content: In vertebrate anatomy, ribs, also known as costae in Latin, are long, curved bones that form the ribcage. In most animals, the ribs encircle the chest, or thorax, and serve to protect vital internal organs such as the lungs, heart, and other structures within the thoracic cavity. In certain species, such as snakes, ribs may extend along the entire body, providing structural support and protection. In human anatomy, both males and females possess a total of 24 ribs, arranged in 12 pairs. The first seven pairs of ribs are referred to as true ribs because they each have their own direct cartilage connections to the sternum. The remaining five pairs are classified as false ribs. Among these, the first three pairs of false ribs share a common cartilage connection to the sternum. The last two pairs, known as the eleventh and twelfth ribs, are called floating ribs (costae fluitantes) or vertebral ribs. These floating ribs are attached only to the vertebrae and do not connect to the sternum or any cartilage extending from the sternum. It is worth noting that some individuals may naturally lack one of the two pairs of floating ribs, while others may have an additional, third pair. The surgical removal of ribs, known as rib excision, may be performed for therapeutic or cosmetic purposes. The ribcage is anatomically separated from the lower abdominal cavity by the thoracic diaphragm, a muscular structure that plays a critical role in respiration. In other animals, the presence and structure of ribs vary significantly. In mammals, ribs are typically associated with the chest region. However, during embryonic development, remnants of ribs can also be observed fused to the cervical (neck) vertebrae and sacral vertebrae. In reptiles, ribs may be present along the entire vertebral column, extending from the neck to the sacrum. Turtles exhibit a unique adaptation in which their ribs are modified into the bony or cartilaginous structures of the carapace (upper shell) and plastron (lower shell). In fish, the number of ribs can vary widely, with some species, such as herring, having up to four ribs per vertebra. However, not all fish possess this many ribs.
